intro: To see revision history in Google Sheets on a Mac, open the sheet in Chrome or Edge, click Last edit at the top right, then pick an earlier version in the right-hand panel. Press ⌘ ⌥ ⇧ H to open the same panel from the keyboard, and make sure you have edit access, because view only links do not show history.
tldr: Open the sheet in Chrome or Edge, then click Last edit at the top right.
Pick an earlier version in the right-hand panel to preview it. Nothing changes until you restore.
Use Restore this version, then Restore, to roll the sheet back. Make a copy first if you need today's version.
Press ⌘ ⌥ ⇧ H to open revision history without reaching for the mouse.
You need edit access. View only links do not show version history.

blocks.text: Google Sheets runs in a web browser on your Mac. The official Google pages I checked describe it as a browser app, and none of them list a Mac app. So the steps here assume Chrome or Edge, with the Sheets page open like any other website. Google does not publish version numbers for the web app, so these steps match the layout on Google's help pages as I checked them on 7 November 2026. If Google moves a button, the button's name is your best guide.
Before you start: edit access and the right browser

Revision history needs edit access. If someone shared a view only link with you, the Last edit link will not show earlier versions. Google's help says view only access does not show version history at all. Ask the owner for Editor rights, or ask them to restore the version for you.

Pick the browser on purpose. Google's offline setup page names Chrome and Microsoft Edge for Docs, Sheets, and Slides. It does not name Safari. I did not test Safari, so if the panel misbehaves there, open the same file in Chrome and compare what you see.

items: Edit access to the spreadsheet, not view only access
Chrome or Microsoft Edge on the Mac
A file that stays within Google's size limits

blocks.text: Size matters more than most people expect. Google's Drive help says a Sheets file can hold up to 20 million cells or 100MB. If your file is near either limit, consider splitting it into smaller files before you depend on long version history.
Open revision history from the Last edit link

Start at the top right of the sheet. Google's help says to click Last edit there. A panel opens on the right, and it lists the earlier versions of the file. Click one, and the sheet shows that version. Only the preview changes. Your current file stays the same until you restore.

Preview before you act. Click two or three versions and read the numbers. Check the tab names, the totals, and any formula you rely on. People often restore the first version they see, then find a second problem. A short look at a few versions first costs very little.

If you prefer the keyboard, press ⌘ ⌥ ⇧ H. Google's keyboard shortcut list gives that combination for Open revision history on Mac. Use it when your hands are already on the keys and you want the panel without moving to the top right of the window.
Restore an older version without losing work

Restoring rolls the live sheet back to the version you picked. Google's help says to click Restore this version, then confirm with Restore. Anyone else who opens the file will see the older content once the restore finishes.

A restore has a cost you should plan for. Google says a restore clears the cell by cell edit history for changes made before it. If you may need that history later, copy the file first. A copy keeps the current state in its own file.

Here is a common case. A budget sheet loses a total on Tuesday. You open revision history, find the Monday version, and make a copy named Budget Monday. You compare the two totals, type the one number you need back into the live sheet, and leave the rest alone.

To make the copy, click More next to the version, choose Make a copy, enter a name, choose a location, and click OK. Google also lets you share the copy with the same people. You can skip that step if you only need the numbers for yourself.
Name versions so you can find them later

Named versions are the checkpoints you can find again. Open More next to a version and choose Name this version. Type a label that says why it matters, such as Before client review. Google's help says each spreadsheet can hold up to 15 named versions.
Use the filter when the list gets long. Turn on Only show named versions, and the panel hides the unnamed entries. Turn it off when you want the full list back.
Fifteen slots go fast on a sheet that changes all week. Name a version before a big change, such as an import or a restructure. That way the label sits on the file you will want to return to.
Mistakes people make with Sheets version history

items: Clicking Last edit on a view only file and expecting history. Ask for edit access first.
Restoring before making a copy, then needing the old cell history later.
Naming a version after the damage is done instead of before the change.
Trusting Show edit history for row, column, format, or formula changes.
Choosing Delete forever when you only wanted to tidy the list.

blocks.text: See who changed one cell, and what that view misses

The version list tracks the whole file. If you only want to know who typed a number, use the cell route instead. Right-click the cell and choose Show edit history. Google's help says this shows who changed the cell.

The cell route has gaps. Google lists these exceptions: added or deleted rows and columns, format changes, formula-driven changes, and changes made before a restore. If the cell history looks thin, check the version list for a structural change.

blocks.text: Pick the route by the question you are asking. Who edited one cell points you to the cell route. What the sheet looked like last week points to the version list. Did someone change the layout points to the version list too, because the cell route skips structural changes.
When version history is missing or empty
Start with access. View only access does not show earlier versions, and Google says so on its help page. Ask the owner to give you edit rights, then reopen the file in Chrome or Edge.

A new file can show little history. Third-party guides suggest making an edit and waiting one or two minutes before the list fills. I could not confirm that advice on Google's pages, so treat it as something to test, not a fix you can count on.

If you are on a phone, switch to a desktop browser. Third-party guides say the mobile app shows less detail. Google's pages I checked do not make that claim, so check it yourself if the detail matters for your work.
How long Google keeps history, and how deleting works

I could not find a retention period for Sheets version history on Google's pages. Third-party sites disagree, and some say the history is kept indefinitely. Do not plan around either claim. Name or copy any version you need to keep.

Deleting is a separate action, and it is permanent. Google's help lists Delete history in the version panel, with Delete forever as the final step. Google says that option is for owners with personal accounts, so a work account may not show it.
Next steps once you find the version you need

Choose one of three moves. Restore the version when the whole sheet should go back. Make a copy when you need both versions side by side. Leave the file alone when you only needed to see an old value. Then decide whether the name or the copy should stay for the next person who opens the file.

faq.question: Is there a Google Sheets app for Mac?
faq.answer: Not one that Google's pages describe. The help pages I checked call Sheets a browser app and do not list a native Mac app. Use Chrome or Edge on your Mac, and open the sheet from Google Drive. Google's offline setup page names Chrome and Edge, not Safari.

faq.question: Where is version history in Google Sheets on Mac?
faq.answer: Click Last edit at the top right of the sheet. Some third-party guides list File > Version history > See version history. I could not confirm that path on Google's pages, so start with Last edit. If the link is missing, check your edit access first.

faq.question: How far back can I see revision history in Google Sheets?
faq.answer: Google's pages I checked do not give a retention period. Third-party sites disagree, so do not count on a version staying forever. If a version matters to you, name it or make a copy now.

faq.question: Can I see version history with view only access?
faq.answer: No. Google's help says you need edit permission to browse earlier versions, and view only access does not show the history. Ask the owner for edit rights, or ask them to restore the version for you.

faq.question: Does restoring an old version delete my current work?
faq.answer: Restoring rolls the live sheet back to the version you picked. Google says a restore clears cell edit history for changes made before it. If you might need the current state, make a copy first, then restore the older version.

faq.question: How many named versions can a Google Sheets file keep?
faq.answer: Google's help says up to 15 named versions per spreadsheet. The same page lists 40 named versions for a Google Doc. The Sheets limit is the smaller one, so plan your labels around 15.

faq.question: What is the size limit for a Google Sheets file?
faq.answer: Google's Drive help says a Sheets file can hold up to 20 million cells or 100MB. If your file is near either limit, split it into smaller files before you rely on long version history.

faq.question: Why does Show edit history skip a change I made?
faq.answer: The cell route misses added or deleted rows and columns, format changes, formula-driven changes, and changes made before a restore. Open the version list and compare versions for those changes instead.

faq.question: Can I delete version history, and can I get it back?
faq.answer: You can delete it, and Google says the deletion is permanent. The Delete forever option is for owners with personal accounts. Name or copy the versions you need before you delete anything.

steps.name: Open the sheet in Chrome or Edge
steps.text: Open the spreadsheet from Google Drive at drive.google.com in Chrome or Edge on your Mac. Sign in to the account that has edit access. Wait until the sheet finishes loading before you go on.
steps.tip: A view only link will not show version history. Ask the owner for Editor rights.

steps.name: Open revision history
steps.text: Click Last edit at the top right of the sheet. Google's help describes this link as the way in. You can also press the keyboard shortcut to open the same panel without the mouse.
steps.tip: If you cannot find Last edit, check your access level first.

steps.name: Read the version list
steps.text: A panel opens on the right. It lists earlier versions of the file. Scroll the list to find the date you need, then click a version to preview it in the sheet.

steps.name: Check the preview
steps.text: Look at the cells, tab names, and totals in the preview. The current sheet does not change until you restore a version or make a copy. Click another version to compare.

steps.name: Restore the version (optional)
steps.text: Click Restore this version, then click Restore to confirm. The live sheet goes back to the version you picked. Make a copy first if you might need today's version.
steps.tip: A restore clears cell edit history for changes made before it.

steps.name: Make a copy instead
steps.text: Click More next to the version you want. Choose Make a copy, enter a name, choose a location, optionally share with the same people, and click OK.

steps.name: Name a version
steps.text: Click More next to a version and choose Name this version. Type a label that says why the version matters. Each spreadsheet can hold up to 15 named versions.
steps.tip: Name versions before a big change, so the label sits on the file you want to return to.

steps.name: Show only named versions
steps.text: Turn on Only show named versions to hide the unnamed entries in the list. Turn it off when you want the full list back.

steps.name: Check the history for one cell
steps.text: Right-click the cell you care about and choose Show edit history. The panel shows who changed that cell. Row and column changes, format changes, and formula-driven changes may not appear here.

steps.name: Close the panel and check the sheet
steps.text: Close the version panel to return to the current sheet. Check which version you are looking at before you type anything, especially after a preview.

troubleshooting.problem: The Last edit link is missing
troubleshooting.fix: Check that you have edit access. Google's help says view only access does not show version history. Ask the owner for Editor rights, then reload the page.

troubleshooting.problem: The version list is empty or very short
troubleshooting.fix: A new file can show little history. Third-party guides suggest making an edit and waiting one or two minutes. I could not confirm that on Google's pages, so make one small edit, wait a moment, then reopen the panel.

troubleshooting.problem: Show edit history does not show a change
troubleshooting.fix: The cell route skips row and column changes, format changes, formula-driven changes, and changes before a restore. Open the version list and compare versions for those.
A restore clears cell edit history made before it. Next time, make a copy first. For this file, check whether a copy or an earlier named version still has what you need.

troubleshooting.problem: A button is not where this page says
troubleshooting.fix: Google does not publish version numbers for the web app, so read the button names rather than the positions. Google's help pages show the current layout. Start again from Last edit.
I did not test Safari, and Google's offline setup page lists Chrome and Edge. Open the same file in Chrome or Edge and compare before you restore anything.
